stances.claim: Three years ago, CJP's wife Leni passed from this world. Since then, CJP has continued living more deliberately while drawing strength from his children and the people around him. Just when none anticipated it, the fragility of life struck again with the passing of his 'lovely balae,' Linda Manuel Mañalac, on March 21 2026 -- her 40th day in heaven approaching.

Tears flowed, yet the memories of her generosity in the minds and hearts of those around her have begun to outweigh the grief. Listening to the eulogies, CJP realized her generosity took many forms. To borrow her son Carlos 'Pop' Mañalac's vivid language, Linda 'spent the last days of her life -- as she always lived -- with complete, absolute, unconditional love ... because of her generosity ... we, her children, are at peace -- grief has been turned to gratitude, and pain into peace.'

To grandchildren/nephews/nieces -- per common apo Andrea -- she was unfailingly generous with affection and time. Nephew Rico Manuel (Ayala Land top executive) shared: 'We lost our Dad and Mom very early ... but we were never truly alone. Ninang Linda was incredibly generous -- not just with what she had, but even more with her time, her attention, and her sincere care.' Even beyond family, Sonya Garcia recalled how 30 years ago, looking only at Sonya's 'anxious eyes and salivating mouth,' Linda pulled out her checkbook and paid the full price for a Cavite estate for 'penniless me' -- 'and presto, the now famous Sonya's Garden was born and later boomed and bloomed.'

Linda hosted Christmas lunch for the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary for over 30 years -- 25 in Pasay and 5 in Forbes Park -- per Sister Cho Borromeo: 'they were far more than simple meals; they were sanctuaries of memory that gave us strength during our most trying times.' Addressing Linda, Sister Cho added: 'Despite your wealthy background, you moved through the world with a profound heart for the poor ... You were famously stingy with yourself, yet you were incredibly lavish with your generosity towards others.' Fr. Robert Manansala of Santuario de San Antonio Parish exclaimed that Linda's greatest treasures of the heart were 'God, family, and other relatives, the Southeastern College community, her wide circles of friends, especially the poor and underprivileged.' The one message that kept resounding: she is 'Generosity Personified.'

CJP had the privilege of personally witnessing her spontaneity, generosity, and magnanimity. At one of her birthday parties, an esteemed visitor she had met for the first time remarked on how lovely her pearl necklace was. Immediately, she gently removed the necklace and placed it around the neck of her stunned visitor, saying 'There, bagay na bagay sa iyo.' Linda and Tong's homes in Makati and Batangas were always open to friends dropping by for a day or a week, complete with household staff and abundance in cupboards/freezers. Fishermen with freshly caught lobsters and crabs near their Punta Fuego home would wait for her, knowing she paid them more than their asking prices to help them provide for their cash-strapped families.

Though not too liturgical, she was definitely spiritual in putting to practice the Ignatian teaching of 'giving without counting the cost and of working without asking for reward, save that of knowing and following the Lord's holy will.' Indeed, she taught by deed not words, by example not trumpets -- without fanfare and drumrolls.

To perpetuate her legacy of unconditional love, all of us -- her friends and relatives -- should strive to follow her quiet, unadulterated generosity and pure magnanimity. Let us seek to imitate her unfettered kindness -- to paraphrase the Good Book -- to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, and visit the prisoners. In doing so, we keep her generous spirit alive, magnified through the lives we touch.

To Tong Mañalac, and to all widows and widowers, may we always look back on the past with gratitude and quiet surrender. Tong, Linda, Leni, and CJP were a 'Happy Foursome.' We were not just friends. We were not just relatives. We were soulmates! Together, we laughed, dined, danced, traveled, celebrated. Painful as it is to live now with only their memory, CJP is certain their spouses would want us to move forward -- to carry on, to live life fully, as they did -- until the day God calls us, in His time, to a joyful reunion with them, together with all His angels in His Heavenly Kingdom.

notable_anecdotes: The Sonya's Garden origin story -- 30 years ago, Linda 'without inspecting the property but looking only at my anxious eyes and salivating mouth, she pulled out her checkbook and paid the full price for penniless me. And presto, the now famous Sonya's Garden was born and later boomed and bloomed' -- among the most vivid friendship-philanthropy origin-stories in CJP's tribute corpus, with the 'anxious eyes and salivating mouth' detail an unusually visual touch.

The birthday-party pearl-necklace anecdote -- Linda removing her own necklace and placing it on a first-met visitor saying 'There, bagay na bagay sa iyo' -- a captured instant of spontaneous-generosity-with-personal-possessions that defies the giving-from-excess paradigm.

The Punta Fuego fishermen routinely paid above their asking prices for lobsters and crabs to help cash-strapped families -- quiet-routine-generosity-with-the-poor that contrasts with one-off philanthropy.

The Sister Cho 'famously stingy with yourself, yet incredibly lavish with your generosity towards others' framing -- captured paradox of self-restraint-plus-other-lavishness as Linda's character signature.

The 30-year Franciscan Missionaries of Mary Christmas-lunch hosting (25 years in Pasay + 5 in Forbes Park) -- a striking decades-spanning institutional commitment that survived multiple home-relocations.

Carlos 'Pop' Mañalac son-eulogy verbatim -- 'grief has been turned to gratitude, and pain into peace' -- among the most quotable son-eulogy compressions of mourning-transformation captured in CJP's column.

Rico Manuel (Ayala Land top executive) 'We lost our Dad and Mom very early ... but we were never truly alone. Ninang Linda was incredibly generous -- not just with what she had, but even more with her time, her attention, and her sincere care' -- captures the orphan-substitute-aunt role Linda played for her nephews/nieces.

The 'even from the vendors on the roads to Tagaytay, from whom Linda bought boiled corn and camote' detail -- extending the generosity-witness list down to the humblest economic-class roadside vendors.

The Ignatian teaching reference 'giving without counting the cost and of working without asking for reward' -- captures the Prayer of Generosity (Suscipe) of St. Ignatius of Loyola as Linda's lived spirituality framework.
The 'taught by deed and not by words, by example and not by trumpets -- without fanfare and drumrolls' formulation -- among CJP's tightest catalogs of quiet-virtue characterization.
The 'Happy Foursome' designation for Tong + Linda + Leni + CJP -- establishes the inter-couple soulmate-bond as collective identity, not merely individual friendship.

The 'We were not just friends. We were not just relatives. We were soulmates!' titular line -- three-rising-tier characterization (friends → relatives → soulmates) that gives the column its title and titular-emotional payoff.

The closing 'until the day God calls us, in His time, to a joyful reunion with them, together with all His angels in His Heavenly Kingdom' -- CJP's eschatological-reunion closing-framing for widow/widower hope.
